A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same watermarking framework and algorithms despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 Section 5 reports original detection, token-replacement robustness and false-alarm experiments using Llama2-13B and Mistral-8×7B.

after.justification: v3 Section 6 and Appendix J retain original experiments and add low-FPR detection, text-quality, runtime, surrogate-model and prompt-availability results.

M1.justification: DAWA names the existing algorithm. v1 Algorithms 1–2 and v3 Appendix I retain NTP-dependent auxiliary sampling, the redundant state, shared Gumbel randomness and surrogate-model detection. The uniform-auxiliary alternative is also retained; expanded explanations and formal revisions do not establish a changed procedure.

E1.justification: v3 adds Wikipedia watermark detection and WMT19 machine-translation evaluation to the retained C4 news-generation and ELI5 question-answering coverage. These introduce an encyclopedic domain and a distinct translation task. Appendix J also explicitly tests detection with and without attached prompts.

E2.justification: KGW-1, EXP-edit and Gumbel-Max remain the evaluated watermarking baselines, including all corresponding clean and attacked comparisons in Tables 1–2. They are reused in the added comparisons. Revised Gumbel-Max scores do not establish a change to the comparator method.

E3.justification: The false-alarm study's description changes from 8,000 watermarked sentences with T=50 in v1 to 100,000 unwatermarked sentences with T=200 in v3 Appendix J, retaining η=0.1. New protocols include Wikipedia evaluation down to FPR 10^-5, BLEU/perplexity evaluation, 500-text timing comparisons and additional model/prompt configurations. These are reported protocol changes, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained token-replacement test, v3 Appendix J adds a cross-family surrogate case using GPT-J-6B/GPT-2 Large, direct comparisons with and without prompts under clean and attacked conditions, and generation-overhead measurements. These examine practical dependencies and costs absent from v1. The existing false-alarm analysis is also revised.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, run seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. References to hash seeds concern watermark sampling. Larger evaluation samples in v3 change the evaluation design, not uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical entries are unchanged. Table 2 substantially revises Gumbel-Max results: Llama2-13B/C4 ROC-AUC rises from 0.776 to 0.968 under the same stated attack, while the proposed method's scores remain unchanged. v3 adds Wikipedia results, including DAWA TPR 0.882 at FPR 10^-5, plus quality, runtime, GPT-J and prompt-comparison results. False-alarm values are replaced under revised settings.

T1.justification: v3 revises Theorem 2's mapping codomain from V^T to a strict superset, explicitly accommodating rejection-only auxiliary values already used in v1's construction. The suboptimal-detector example changes its premise from an injective mapping to a surjective mapping. Appendices B–D also address continuous auxiliary spaces more explicitly. The principal error bounds and semantic-robustness results remain.

C1.justification: The joint-optimality, practical surrogate-based detection and semantic-robustness contributions remain. v3 adds an explicit introductory claim of superior detection at extremely low false-positive rates and makes distribution-adaptive auxiliary sampling the central stated design takeaway.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly qualifies that token-level optimality need not imply sequence-level optimality. It also argues from the new experiments that tokenizer compatibility matters more than model-family membership and that prompt absence has little effect. New quality and runtime discussions interpret the results as preserving text quality with negligible generation overhead.

D1.justification: v3 newly describes empirical ROC-based threshold selection, identifies GPT-3 and MBART for quality evaluation, specifies the 774-million-parameter GPT-2 Large surrogate, and reports generation timings. The core A100 hardware, η=0.2, T=200 and algorithm disclosures remain. No new code or data release information is supplied.

R1.justification: v3 adds classical watermarking references by Merhav and collaborators, Thorisson's coupling reference, and citations supporting the new quality experiments; Cover and Thomas is removed. It emphasizes adaptive auxiliary distributions relative to fixed classical watermarks, while retaining the main positioning against Huang et al. and Li et al.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and framework-to-algorithm narrative are extensively revised around DAWA. Algorithms and experiments become separate sections. The construction example, pseudocode and semantic-robustness section move into reorganized appendices, and an Impact Statement is added.

P2.justification: The main text switches to two columns, the overview diagram is redrawn, and new ROC and DAWA-workflow figures are introduced. Quality and supplementary-analysis tables are added, while the construction figure and pseudocode move to appendices. Tables 1–2 are compressed into much smaller side-by-side displays.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical support for practicality that v1 largely left to detection results and theoretical arguments. Table 3 examines text quality, while Appendix J measures overhead and tests surrogate compatibility and prompt dependence. The new low-FPR evaluation and explicitly unwatermarked false-alarm sample also improve validation of a central operating requirement. Formal revisions better accommodate the redundant-state construction. Sparse protocol and uncertainty reporting, unexplained baseline-score revisions and cramped tables temper these gains, but the added validation addresses substantial gaps in v1.
